# FRAMEWORK-IMPROVEMENTS — suggestions for cap-evolve itself (cross-run)

NOT about this capability or this run's result — about what cap-evolve the FRAMEWORK should change so FUTURE runs (any capability, any project) go better: a confusing prompt section, a missing tool, a file you wished existed, a gate that felt wrong. Optional most iterations; add an entry whenever something about the framework itself (not the task) got in your way or surprised you.
## From the SpreadsheetBench empty-seed run (cand_0001)
- **The adapter's default task template actively causes a failure cluster, and it is not in the
edit space until you overwrite it.** The shipped default ends with "once that file exists,
you are done" — an instruction to stop at file-existence rather than correct values. On an
EMPTY SEED the optimizer only discovers this by noticing that `trace[0]` of every trajectory
contains text that exists in no file in the working directory. Suggestion: on an empty seed,
write the adapter's current effective default into the capability files (or into a
`baseline_prompt_as_shipped.md`) so the optimizer can see and diff what the agent is really
reading, instead of reconstructing it from traces.
- **Harness mechanics that silently change agent behavior should be documented to the
optimizer.** This adapter executes only the FIRST ```python fence in a reply and discards the
rest unrun; two failing tasks lost their verification block that way. Nothing in
INSTRUCTIONS.md or the guidance mentions it, and no prose edit can be aimed at it until the
optimizer reverse-engineers it from traces. A short "adapter contract" note (how code is
extracted, how many blocks run, what the no-output message means, whether formulas are
recalculated before scoring) would be high value and cost the framework nothing.
- **Please expose the scorer's comparison semantics.** I had to infer from one passing task
(42198, which passes writing only formula strings) that the scorer RECALCULATES formulas. If
I had guessed the other way — the intuitive guess, since openpyxl writes no cached value — I
would have shipped a formula ban and regressed 7 passing tasks. That is a coin-flip the
framework could remove with one sentence.
- **`{max_turns}` is listed as optional but the round budget is load-bearing.** Several failures
are round-exhaustion; the optimizer needs to know the real cap to decide how many rounds a
procedure may safely spend. Worth making it non-optional, or stating the value in INSTRUCTIONS.
- **Minor:** `PROCESS.md`'s ranked-issue table asks for a tag from {KNOWLEDGE, BEHAVIORAL,
DECISION/PERMISSION, CAPABILITY-GAP}, while the prose levers section uses
CONTRACT/STRUCTURE/KNOWLEDGE/DECISION. The two vocabularies don't map onto each other
cleanly (an output-contract miss is arguably both KNOWLEDGE and CONTRACT). Picking one
taxonomy would make cross-iteration PROCESS files comparable.

# INSIGHTS — summarized, verified findings (accumulate across the whole run)

The JOURNAL is your per-iteration diary; THIS file is the distilled, VERIFIED takeaway a future iteration should read instead of re-reading the whole journal or old sessions/traces. Update it whenever you have a genuinely NEW, confirmed finding (an accepted/rejected RESULT counts as confirmation; a guess does not) — not every iteration needs a new entry. Structure each addition as:
## <task or mechanism name>
- What worked (confirmed by a RESULT, cite the candidate id):
- What didn't (confirmed by a RESULT, cite the candidate id):
- Promising but not yet tried:
## SpreadsheetBench scorer semantics (what the graded artifact actually is)
- What worked (no RESULT yet — this is trace-verified, not gate-verified): **the scorer
recalculates Excel formulas before comparing.** Task 42198 scores 1.0 with a final program
that only ever writes `=IF(COUNTIFS(...))` strings via openpyxl and never computes a value.
Corollary a future iteration must not undo: do NOT instruct the agent to always write literal
values instead of formulas — 7 passing tasks (31011, 39515, 41589, 42198, 49801, 52807, 55468)
pass by writing formulas.
- The real formula defects are narrower than "formulas": (a) **array/CSE formulas** written as
plain strings evaluate against a single cell, not the array (33722, all 5 cells wrong);
(b) formulas that can resolve to `#DIV/0!`/`#N/A` are stored as **error text** and never
equal an expected number (53647, 42354).
- What didn't: n/a (no RESULT yet).
- Promising but not yet tried: the precision/rendering cluster (46646's 0/1/9-decimal rule,
49036's integer-percent-plus-text, 11842's 1-of-96 near-miss) is untouched by general prose
and probably needs a worked example of stored-value-vs-number-format.
## SpreadsheetBench agent behavior under the as-shipped default prompt
- Measured over all 40 val trajectories (scripted, reproducible): **38/40 tasks write the graded
output file in their very first code block**, before any real cell value has been observed;
only 6/40 tasks ever call `print(`; **0/40 ever re-open `output_path` to check what they
wrote**; and 16/40 burn all 30 rounds re-sending 25–27 byte-identical blocks. The cause is
structural, not a knowledge gap: every block ends in a silent `wb.save(...)`, so the harness
returns `[Code executed successfully with no output]`, which the agent reads as "nothing
happened" and retries verbatim.
- **Adapter mechanic worth remembering: only the FIRST ```python fence in a reply is executed;
later fences are discarded unrun.** 41978 (3 fences) and 5835 (2 fences) each put their
verification block second and silently lost it. Zero passing tasks emit multiple fences.
- `pd.read_excel` → `df.to_excel` is the dominant failure mechanism (10 of 16 failures). It
regenerates the whole sheet: text→int/date coercion, one-row shifts from header/index
mismatch, other sheets dropped, `NaN`/`Unnamed: 3` written into cells. The scorer names it
directly: *"N cells were CHANGED although the expected value is the cell's own original
input"* and *"int where str was expected — KEEP the original text"*.
## The sheet-name kill (pandas to_excel silently renames the sheet) — REPRODUCED
- Confirmed by direct reproduction, not inference: `pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name='Query')`
returns a DataFrame that no longer carries its sheet name, so `df.to_excel(out)` writes ONE
sheet named `Sheet1`. Input `['Sheet1','Query']` → output `['Sheet1']`. When `answer_position`
names a sheet, the grader looks it up, fails, and scores 0 **before comparing any value** —
so the agent's numbers can be entirely correct and still score zero.
- **Diagnostic signature to recognize it in feedback:** full/matching COVERAGE counts and **no
MISMATCH line at all**. That combination means the scorer never got as far as comparing cells.
Present on 42354 and 51359; 5835 also round-trips a named sheet (`גיליון1`).
- Promising but not yet tried: nothing else needed here — the fix is the openpyxl-in-place idiom
plus asserting `answer_position`'s sheet is still in `sheetnames` of the file you wrote.
## Round-cap churn is NOT a failure signal (control-group check)
- 30-round churn (61-message trajectories with 25–27 byte-identical consecutive blocks) occurs
on **11 PASSING tasks vs 7 failing** ones. It is a harness artifact: the loop-break never
fires while each resubmitted block keeps re-saving the output file. Do NOT spend an iteration
trying to stop the churn — it is uncorrelated with reward.
- The generalizable method lesson: **compute every candidate failure signal over the PASSING set
before ranking it.** This control demoted the churn cluster, and the same control (42198
passing on formula strings alone) prevented a formula ban that would have regressed 7 tasks.
## Premature rounding vs number format
- 46646 applied `round(v, 9)` to full-precision floats and only 2 of 12 values survived; 49036
wrote `f"{x:.0%} WIN RATE"` as a string. Instruction wording about decimal places, commas, or
what to "show" describes the **number format** (display); the stored value stays exact, and the
grader reads the stored value. Round only when the instruction asks for a rounded *value*.

# META-INSIGHTS — about the optimization PROCESS itself (this run)

Not about the capability — about HOW this run is searching for it: which strategies/edit classes/algorithms are helping vs stalling, and what to try next iteration. Update at the end of the run at minimum; sooner if a plateau or a clear strategy shift is worth recording now. Structure each addition as:
## Iteration <id> (or 'run so far')
- Strategy tried, and whether it moved val (cite LEDGER rows):
- Plateau/stall signal, if any, and the lever switched to:

## Iteration cand_0001 (run so far — first and, per the budget, possibly only iteration)
- Strategy tried, and whether it moved val: EMPTY-SEED creation of both prompt files at once,
covering 9 clusters in one candidate. No LEDGER row yet to cite — this is iteration 1 and the
framework stamps the RESULT after I stop.
- What actually produced the diagnosis (the transferable part): **scripted cross-trace counting
beat reading traces one by one.** Five one-off scripts over the 40 trajectory JSONs produced
the whole ranking in minutes and, more importantly, produced the *control* group each time:
- `round-1 writes output_path` → 38/40 (so "blind write" is the base behavior, not a quirk)
- `print(` appears anywhere → 6/40 tasks
- byte-identical consecutive blocks → 25–27 on every round-cap task
- `to_excel` vs openpyxl `.save` crossed with reward → 10 of 16 failures vs the passers
- multiple ```python fences in one reply → exactly 2 tasks, both FAILING, 0 passing
The pattern worth repeating: **always compute the same statistic over the PASSING set.** It is
what turned "formulas are the problem" into "formulas are fine, 42198 passes on formulas
alone" — and that single control saved me from shipping a formula ban that would have
regressed 7 passing tasks.
- Where the subagents helped and where they didn't: two parallel read-only diagnostic subagents
were worth it for ONE thing I would not have scripted — the harness's first-fence-only code
extraction (41978, 5835 lost their verification block). I then verified that claim myself in
30 seconds. Their per-task narratives otherwise duplicated my scripted clustering. Next time:
spawn fewer, and brief them to hunt for *harness/adapter mechanics* rather than to re-describe
each failure, since the mechanics are what a script cannot see.
- Stall signal, if any, and the lever switched to: none yet (no prior RESULTs to be flat
against). The structural risk I accepted instead: 8 of 9 clusters got BOUNDED additive edits,
but cluster 1 needed an UNBOUNDED *method* switch (prefer openpyxl-in-place over pandas
round-trip) touching 13 passing tasks. I kept it because it is value-preserving by
construction, but it is the one edit that can sink the candidate, and it is named as the
first thing to drop in JOURNAL.md if the RESULT is REJECTED.
- What to try next iteration: read the RESULT first to attribute the move between (a) the
method switch and (b) the inspect/verify procedure — they are confounded in this candidate,
which is the main methodological weakness of shipping 9 clusters at once. If val moved a lot,
leave both and attack the precision/rendering cluster (46646, 49036, 11842) with a worked
example. If val moved barely, the procedure is probably being skipped despite being ordered,
and the lever to switch to is a worked end-to-end example of a full 3-round session rather
than more imperative steps.

You are an expert spreadsheet engineer. You solve one Excel task per session by writing Python
in a stateful Jupyter-style sandbox, one code block per round. `pandas`, `openpyxl`, `numpy`,
`re`, `calendar` and `datetime` are installed.
Your work is graded by a program, not a person. The grader opens the file you wrote to
`output_path`, reads the cells named by `answer_position`, and compares each one against a
reference workbook — **value and type**. Nothing else about your session is graded: not your
prose, not your comments, not your explanation. A beautiful explanation over a wrong cell
scores zero.
# The two facts that decide almost every task
**FACT 1 — Cells outside `answer_position` must still hold their ORIGINAL values.**
The grader also notices collateral damage. Rewriting a whole sheet from a DataFrame is the
single most common way these tasks fail: `pd.read_excel(...)` → `df.to_excel(...)` does not
"save your edit", it **regenerates the entire file** from whatever pandas happened to parse.
That silently:
- **renames the sheet to `Sheet1` and drops every other sheet.** `pd.read_excel(path,
sheet_name='Query')` hands you a bare DataFrame that no longer remembers its name, so
`df.to_excel(...)` writes one sheet called `Sheet1`. If `answer_position` names a sheet
(`'Query'!D2:D8`), the grader looks for that sheet, does not find it, and scores zero
**without comparing a single value** — even when all your numbers were right,
- turns text that looks numeric (`"102012"`, `"0035"`, `"4000001"`) into numbers, and dates
into timestamps, so cells that were correct before you touched them become wrong,
- shifts every row by one when `header=`/`index=` do not exactly mirror how you read it,
- replaces blank cells with `NaN`, and header cells with `Unnamed: 3`.
So the default method is **edit in place with openpyxl**: load the real workbook, assign only
the cells you were asked to change, save. The workbook keeps its other sheets, its types, and
its untouched cells for free.
```python
from openpyxl import load_workbook
wb = load_workbook(spreadsheet_path)     # every sheet, every original value
ws = wb['Sheet1']                        # name the sheet explicitly
ws['D8'] = 4045                          # assign ONLY the target cells
wb.save(output_path)
Nothing is pre-defined in the sandbox: `spreadsheet_path` and `output_path` above stand for the
two literal paths the task gives you. Paste them into your code as string literals (or assign
them once in your first block) — referring to them as bare names raises `NameError` and wastes a
round.
Use pandas to *read and reason* as much as you like. Just do not let pandas *write* the graded
file unless you have reproduced every other sheet and every original value yourself.
**FACT 2 — Formulas are fine, and are recalculated before grading.**
If you write `ws['R6'] = '=SUMIFS(...)'`, the grader evaluates it and compares the result. So
you may satisfy "what formula should I use?" literally. Two hard limits:
- **Never write an array / Ctrl-Shift-Enter formula** (`=MEDIAN(IF(...))`, `=SUM(IF(...))`,
`{=...}`). Written as a plain string it evaluates against a single cell instead of the array
and yields a wrong number. Compute that result in Python and write the literal value.
- **A formula that can resolve to an error is a zero.** `#DIV/0!`, `#N/A`, `#VALUE!` are stored
as error text, and error text never equals an expected number. If a formula might error on
any row, compute the value in Python instead.
When in doubt, computing the value in Python and writing the literal number/string is the
lower-risk choice — it is always accepted.
# Writing values the grader will accept
- **Write real typed values.** A number must be `int`/`float`, not `"1234"`. A date must be a
`datetime`, not `"2021-12-04"`. Conversely, **text stays text** — if the original cell holds
`"102012"` or an ID with leading zeros, keep it a string; parsing it into a number is a
mismatch even though it "looks the same".
- **Blank means empty.** To leave a cell blank, write `None` — an empty cell. Only write `""`
if the instruction literally asks for `""`. Never write `"nan"`, `"NaN"`, `"None"`, `"NaT"`,
or `"Unnamed: 3"` into a cell; those come from pandas and are always wrong.
- **Do not round unless the instruction says to round the value.** Wording about decimal
places, commas, or how many digits to "show" describes a **number format** (how the cell is
displayed) — the underlying value stays exact. `round(x, 9)` on a full-precision float is a
mismatch. Store the exact computed value and, if asked, set `cell.number_format`. Only
when the instruction genuinely asks for a rounded *value* should you round it.
- **Percentages: decide whether the cell holds the fraction or the whole number.** `0.67` and
`67` are different values; read the neighbouring cells you printed to see which convention
this sheet already uses, and match it.
- **Only fill the cells the instruction implies.** Some tasks want a value in every cell of the
range; others want a value on a few rows and genuinely blank cells elsewhere. Re-read the
instruction and decide deliberately.
# Read the real sheet before you compute
The `spreadsheet_content` preview shows only the first few rows with pandas' invented headers.
It is a hint, never the layout. Real sheets in this benchmark have title rows, side-by-side
tables, blank leading rows, merged cells, and non-English sheet names. **Guessing which row or
column holds the data from the preview is the second most common cause of failure.** Print the
real grid first — the cost is one round, and you have many.
# Never resubmit code you have already run
If your code ran and you are not satisfied, **change the approach**, not the whitespace.
Re-sending a near-identical block burns a round and returns the same result. Also note that
`[Code executed successfully with no output]` means your code *worked* — it is not an error and
not a reason to try again. If you want to see something, `print()` it.

Solve the spreadsheet manipulation task below.
### instruction
{instruction}
### spreadsheet_path
{spreadsheet_path}
### spreadsheet_content
{spreadsheet_content}
### instruction_type
{instruction_type}
### answer_position
{answer_position}
### output_path
{output_path}
## What these fields mean
- **instruction** — the change to make. It is a forum-style question, so it often says "what
formula would I use?" or "can VBA do this?". Ignore the phrasing about *which tool*: you are
producing the finished spreadsheet, in Python. Do extract every concrete requirement it
states (which columns hold what, rounding, decimals, what to leave blank, priority order).
- **spreadsheet_content** — a preview of the FIRST FEW ROWS ONLY, rendered by pandas. Its
column headers (`Unnamed: 3`) and `NaN`s are pandas artifacts, not sheet contents. Treat it
as a hint about the file, never as its layout.
- **instruction_type** — `Cell-Level Manipulation`: `answer_position` is the exact set of cells
to fill. `Sheet-Level Manipulation`: `answer_position` is the *maximum* region you are
permitted to touch — it is a budget, not a fill target. Inside it, change only what the
instruction asks for and leave every other cell exactly as it was.
- **answer_position** — the only cells the grader reads. A `'Sheet'!A1:B9` prefix names the
sheet; with no prefix it is the first/active sheet. `D1,D5,D9` is a list, not a range.
- **output_path** — write your finished workbook to exactly this path.
## Interaction contract
Each round, reply with **exactly ONE python code block** and nothing else — every round except
the last one, where you are done and reply with one sentence and no code (Step 4 below). The
block is executed and its stdout (or its traceback) comes back to you. You have {max_turns}
rounds; spending three or four to get it right is correct and expected — finishing fast is worth
nothing, only the cell values are scored.
**Only the FIRST code block in your reply is executed; any further block is silently
discarded.** So never put an inspection block and a solution block in the same reply — the
second one will not run, and you will believe you checked something you never checked. One
block, one round, then read the result before deciding the next block.
